subject: chemistry
question_text: Compare the dipole moment of NH₃ molecule with that of NF₃ molecule.

verification.note: Chapter 3 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.56-61), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. The numeric values 1.47 D and 0.23 D are the NCERT reference values; the book argues the comparison qualitatively only.

steps.label: Both shapes
lines: NH₃ and NF₃ both have a pyramidal shape,
with one lone pair of electrons on the
N atom.
So the difference in their dipole moments
cannot come from the shape — it comes from
the direction of the bond moments.
steps.why: Establishing that the two shapes are identical rules out geometry as the cause and points the answer at bond-moment directions, which is the actual argument.
common_mistakes: Saying NF₃ is planar. Both molecules are pyramidal.
Forgetting the lone pair on N, whose moment the whole comparison is about.
steps.memory_tip: Same shape, same lone pair — only the arrow directions differ.
steps.margin_note: The one-line setup: same shape, so compare directions.

steps.label: NH₃ directions
lines: In NH₃: N is more electronegative than H,
so each N−H bond moment points from H
toward N.
The resultant of the three N−H bond moments
points in the SAME direction as the lone
pair moment.
The two add, giving a large dipole moment.
steps.why: Both contributions point away from the hydrogens, up through the lone pair, so they reinforce each other and the total moment is large.
common_mistakes: Drawing the N−H moments toward H. The arrow points to the more electronegative atom, which is N.
steps.memory_tip: In NH₃ everything points the same way: bond resultant and lone pair together.
steps.margin_note: The words same direction must appear for this mark.

steps.label: NF₃ directions
lines: In NF₃: F is more electronegative than N,
so each N−F bond moment points from N
toward F.
The resultant of the three N−F bond moments
points OPPOSITE to the lone pair moment.
The two partly cancel, giving a small
dipole moment.
steps.why: Reversing the electronegativity order reverses the bond-moment resultant, so in NF₃ it works against the lone pair moment instead of with it.
common_mistakes: Claiming full cancellation. The cancellation is partial — NF₃ still has a small non-zero moment.
Arguing from bond polarity strength alone. The DIRECTION of the resultant is the point.
steps.memory_tip: In NF₃ the arrows point opposite ways: bond resultant down to F, lone pair up.
steps.margin_note: The words opposite direction must appear for this mark.

steps.label: The comparison

lines.text: μ of NH₃ (1.47 D) > μ of NF₃ (0.23 D)

lines: Adding moments in NH₃ against partly
cancelling moments in NF₃ makes the dipole
moment of NH₃ much greater than that of NF₃.
steps.why: The boxed inequality is the asked comparison; the reference values make the size of the difference concrete.
common_mistakes: Writing the inequality the wrong way round. NH₃ has the larger moment.
steps.memory_tip: Together in NH₃, opposed in NF₃ — so NH₃ is larger.
steps.margin_note: The inequality alone earns the mark; the D values strengthen it.

insider_note: The direction comparison carries the marks: same direction in NH₃, opposite direction in NF₃. State which way each resultant points.
